questions.q: Per this lesson, why is an RPC node well-suited to calls like balanceOf or ownerOf?
options: They're point lookups — one storage slot, one bounded answer — which is exactly what a node is built to serve
Because RPC nodes cache every possible aggregate query in advance
Because balanceOf and ownerOf automatically query a secondary SQL database
They aren't well-suited to it; every call requires scanning the full chain history
questions.explain: A point lookup reads one storage slot for one answer, which is bounded, cheap work for a node — unlike an aggregate, historical question.

questions.q: What three problems does the lesson identify with looping eth_getLogs over block ranges to answer an aggregate question?
options: Provider range/log caps force chunking, every chunk counts against rate limits, and the work is redone from scratch on every request
eth_getLogs is deprecated and no longer callable on any network
It only works for contracts deployed in the last 24 hours
It requires a paid Etherscan API key that most providers don't support
questions.explain: The lesson walks through exactly these three compounding costs: range caps forcing chunked calls, those calls eating the rate-limit quota, and zero reuse of prior work.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what can't you send directly to an RPC node that you could send to a SQL database?
options: A filtered, ordered query like "WHERE balance > 100 ORDER BY timestamp" — nodes have no such query layer over chain state
Any call at all — RPC nodes don't accept structured requests
A request for the current block number
A single balanceOf call for one address
questions.explain: Nodes store current state keyed by contract and slot; there's no built-in filtering/sorting query layer like SQL's WHERE/ORDER BY.

questions.q: What three-step pattern does the lesson say every real fix for this problem follows?
options: Listen for the relevant events, write them into a queryable database, then query that database instead of the chain
Buy a faster RPC provider, increase the rate limit, and keep scanning logs the same way
Store the entire blockchain locally and run SQL directly against the raw block files
Ask users to submit their own transaction history manually
questions.explain: This listen → write → query pattern is the lesson's core takeaway and the job description of every indexer, managed or custom.

questions.q: Why does increasing the speed or rate limit of your RPC provider NOT solve the "every trade this wallet ever made" problem, per this lesson?
options: Because the problem is architectural — nodes don't store a queryable, filterable history shaped for aggregate questions, no matter how fast the calls run
Because faster providers always charge per-query fees that make the feature unprofitable
Because RPC providers refuse to serve historical log data at any speed
It does solve it — a fast enough provider makes log-scanning viable at any contract age
questions.explain: The lesson's point is that the limitation isn't speed, it's that nodes have no indexed, queryable history — so faster calls just mean faster repetition of the same unscalable work.
